A row of five tall display cases has opened along the far wall of the gallery — the Culture Cases. Each one holds something a different group of people brought to this region: a lacrosse stick from the Haudenosaunee, a cacao pod from the Maya, a mission bell from Spanish settlers, an ARRÊT sign from French settlers, and a drum for African heritage. The cases need their stories told carefully and fairly. As Regional Curators, your job today is to match each culture's contribution to the right case, and to do it with courtesy.

📍 WELCOME · ENTER THE MUSEUM
Many Peoples, One Region
🎬
Teacher recording notes: Welcome back. Remind them: "Yesterday we walked the Natural Resources Shelf. Today, we turn from the land to the people who have lived on it." Read the Curator's Question aloud: "Which peoples have settled in North America and the Caribbean, and what did each group bring that still shapes the region today?" Spotlight courtesy: explain that talking about people requires extra care — using specific group names, telling stories accurately, and not lumping everyone together. Mention that Indigenous peoples have been here the longest, and many still live in this region today. Under 2 minutes.
🏛️ Virtue Spotlight — Courtesy
Courtesy in a museum means using a culture's real name — not a lazy or made-up one — and getting the facts right. The Haudenosaunee are not the same as the Maya. Spanish settlers are not the same as French settlers. Curators learn the differences so visitors can too.
🕯️

Your Role Today: You are a Regional Curator — your job is to help visitors see that this region has been home to many peoples, each one bringing something that still shapes the region. Today, you'll match contributions to cultures and write one respectful label.

🔍 TEACHING · EXPLORE
Five Culture Cases
🎬
Teacher recording notes: Walk students through the five culture cases. (1) Haudenosaunee — Indigenous peoples of the Northeast Woodlands, longhouses, the game of lacrosse, the Three Sisters farming (corn, beans, squash). (2) Maya — Indigenous of Mexico and Central America, stepped pyramids, chocolate (cacao), the concept of zero in math. (3) Spanish Colonial — settled Mexico, Florida, Caribbean, and the U.S. Southwest; brought the Spanish language and mission churches. (4) French Settlers — settled Quebec and Louisiana; brought the French language and Catholic traditions. (5) African Heritage — many African peoples were brought to this region against their will and kept their cultures alive; shaped American music (jazz, blues), foods, and farming knowledge. Then introduce the matching activity: students match a contribution to its culture. 3–5 minutes.
1
Learn the Story
📖
Five Cultures of the Region
A respectful look at who came here, and what they brought

North America and the Caribbean has been home to many peoples, far too many for one lesson. Today we meet five of them. All five are still part of the region today.

🥍 The Haudenosaunee (HOH-dee-no-SHOH-nee) — also called the Iroquois — are Indigenous peoples of the Northeast Woodlands. They have lived in what is now New York State, Quebec, and Ontario for over 1,000 years. They built long wooden homes called longhouses, played the game that grew into today's lacrosse, and farmed three crops together that grow well as a team: corn, beans, and squash, called the "Three Sisters."

🍫 The Maya are Indigenous peoples of southern Mexico and Central America. Over 1,000 years ago, they built huge stone cities with stepped pyramids, like the one we visited at Chichén Itzá. The Maya were one of the first peoples in the world to use a sign for zero, and they kept a calendar. They grew cacao and made chocolate drinks long ago. Millions of Maya people still live in Mexico, Guatemala, and Belize today.

🔔 Spanish settlers arrived in this region starting in the late 1400s. They brought the Spanish language and the Catholic faith. They built mission churches with bells across what is now Mexico, the U.S. Southwest, Florida, and the Caribbean. Today, Spanish is one of the most-spoken languages in this region.

⚜️ French settlers arrived in the 1600s. They settled along the St. Lawrence River in what became Quebec, Canada, and along the Mississippi River in what became Louisiana. They brought the French language. Today, Quebec is mostly French-speaking, and you can still hear French words in Louisiana place names.

🥁 African peoples were brought to this region beginning in the 1500s. Most arrived against their will, taken from West and Central Africa as part of the slave trade. Even under terrible conditions, they kept their cultures alive — passing down music, foods, farming knowledge, and stories. American jazz, blues, and gospel music all grew from African musical traditions. Today, African American culture is a deep part of life across the United States and the Caribbean.

This is not the whole list. Many other peoples — the Inuit in the Arctic, the Taíno in the Caribbean, English settlers, Chinese and Italian and many more recent arrivals — have all helped shape this region. Curators tell as much of the story as they can, respectfully.

🤔

Pause & Think: If you only learned about ONE of these cultures, you'd miss most of the story of the region. Why does a good curator make sure visitors meet many cultures, not just one?

Investigate the Map
🗺️
Source Map
Where Each People Lived and Settled
Map Source · A simple map made for this lesson from public-domain Natural Earth map data. The marks show about where each people lived or settled; they are not exact borders.
👁️

What do I see? Find the five kinds of marks in the key. Where are the Haudenosaunee homelands? Where are the Maya lands? Which rivers are next to the French towns?

💭

What does it mean? Indigenous peoples were here for thousands of years before European settlers arrived. Many Indigenous nations are still here today, on the same lands. What does that tell you about how cultures share a region?

⚖️

Why does it matter? Curators show both who was here first and who came later. Why is it important to do both — not just one?

3
Answer the Visitors
🏺
Match Each Contribution to Its Culture
Tap each item, then tap the culture it came from.

The contributions got mixed up between the cases. Read each item carefully and tap the cultural group it belongs to. Each one locks green when you match it right.

Chocolate (cacao): chocolate drinks made from cacao beans, grown long ago in the warm forests of southern Mexico and Central America.
The Three Sisters — the farming method of growing corn, beans, and squash together so they help each other grow. Used by Indigenous nations of the Northeast Woodlands.
Mission churches — small church buildings built across Mexico, Florida, the U.S. Southwest, and the Caribbean, starting in the 1500s.
The French language spoken in Quebec — still the main language of most people in the province of Quebec, Canada.
Jazz and blues music — musical styles that grew up in the southern United States and the Caribbean, rooted in African musical traditions.
Stone stepped pyramids — like the great pyramid at Chichén Itzá in Mexico's Yucatán, built over 1,000 years ago.
🎉 Cases filled!
🔎 Discovery Fact: The Haudenosaunee Great Law of Peace is a set of laws for living together in peace. It was passed down by memory and wampum belts for hundreds of years, and the Haudenosaunee still follow it today. Some historians think it gave ideas to the people who wrote the U.S. Constitution.
⏳

Then & Now: Chocolate from the Maya, lacrosse from the Haudenosaunee, Spanish and French words, jazz from African music: the cultures in these cases didn't end long ago. They're around you every day.

4
Connect the Ideas
🏷️ Exhibit Label

North America and the Caribbean has been home to many peoples. Indigenous nations have been here the longest and are still here today. Spanish, French, English, and other settlers brought languages, religions, and traditions. African peoples — brought against their will — shaped music, food, and farming across the region. Together, these cultures continue to make the region what it is.

🦉
🧭 Opti says…
A curator's tip: when we say "Native American" or "Indigenous," that includes hundreds of different nations — Haudenosaunee, Maya, Inuit, Cherokee, Navajo, and many more. Each has its own language, traditions, and story. Using a specific name is the most respectful thing a curator can do.

You've filled the cases. Let's see how well the cultures stuck.

🧠
Quick Self-Check
🧠

Not graded — just for you! Answer these three questions before writing your evidence responses.

1. Who has lived in this region the LONGEST?
AIndigenous peoples
BSpanish settlers
CFrench settlers
Right! Indigenous peoples — like the Haudenosaunee, Maya, Inuit, and many others — have lived in this region for thousands of years.
European settlers arrived in the 1400s and 1500s. But people were already here, and had been for thousands of years. Who?
2. Which people built stepped stone pyramids, and were one of the first in the world to use a sign for zero?
AThe French
BThe Haudenosaunee
CThe Maya
Yes! The Maya built stone cities with stepped pyramids in Mexico and Central America, and they used a sign for zero. They also grew cacao for chocolate.
Remember the pyramid we visited at Chichén Itzá in Mexico? Which culture built it?
3. Why does courtesy matter when a curator describes a culture?
ASo the labels look nice.
BCultures are real groups of people, so curators use real names and accurate facts.
CTo save time.
Exactly! Cultures aren't just facts in a book — they're living groups of people. Curators take care to get names right and tell stories accurately.
It's not about how labels look or saving time. It's about something deeper. Cultures are made up of real people. What does that tell you?
